appearance_facts.location: The May bar on the far right of the chart
appearance_facts.fact: The May bar is extremely short, appearing as a thin red strip at the bottom of the chart. Its height is visually negligible compared to all other bars, representing a value significantly lower than the 10,000 kWh mark on the y-axis.

appearance_facts.location: The June bar, third from the left
appearance_facts.fact: The June bar is the second shortest on the chart, reaching a height of approximately 17,500 kWh. It is visibly much taller than the May bar.

appearance_facts.location: The January bar, second from the left
appearance_facts.fact: The January bar is the tallest on the chart, reaching the top grid line at 40,000 kWh.

appearance_facts.location: The April bar, first from the left
appearance_facts.fact: The April bar is the second tallest, reaching just below the 30,000 kWh line.

appearance_facts.location: The March bar, fifth from the left
appearance_facts.fact: The March bar reaches a height of approximately 27,000 kWh.

appearance_facts.location: The February bar, fourth from the left
appearance_facts.fact: The February bar reaches a height of approximately 20,000 kWh.

printed_facts.location: X-axis tick labels from left to right
printed_facts.fact: Apr, Jan, Jun, Feb, Mar, May

public_definitions: Review the monthly grid energy dashboard and decide whether May should be handled as a standard low-usage case or escalated as a critical low-usage anomaly for this reporting cycle.
uncertain: The exact numerical value for the May bar is not printed on the chart, only its relative height is visible.
